questions.q: Which muscle is the principal muscle of quiet (tidal) inspiration, and what nerve supplies it?
options: External intercostal muscles, supplied by T1-T11 intercostal nerves
Diaphragm, supplied by the phrenic nerves (C3, C4, C5)
Internal intercostal muscles, supplied by the vagus nerve
Sternocleidomastoid, supplied by the spinal accessory nerve (CN XI)
questions.explain: Contraction of the dome-shaped diaphragm (innervated by C3-C5 via the phrenic nerve) pulls the central tendon downward, accounting for ~75% of the intrathoracic volume increase during quiet inspiration.

open.q: Name the primary muscle of quiet inspiration, its motor nerve supply, and the spinal cord root levels of that nerve.
accept: Diaphragm; phrenic nerve (C3, C4, C5)
Diaphragm supplied by C3-C5 phrenic nerve

questions.q: How do the external intercostal muscles expand the thoracic cavity during inspiration?
options: They depress the ribs to reduce thoracic volume
They elevate ribs: pump-handle increases AP diameter; bucket-handle increases transverse diameter
They elevate upper ribs to increase transverse diameter and lower ribs to increase AP diameter
They contract mainly during forced expiration to compress the lungs
questions.explain: External intercostals elevate the ribs outward and upward, enlarging both the anteroposterior and transverse diameters of the rib cage alongside vertical descent of the diaphragm. External intercostal fibres run downwards and forwards. Their contraction elevates the ribs: pump-handle movement raises the sternum and upper ribs to increase anteroposterior diameter, while bucket-handle movement swings the lower ribs outward to increase transverse diameter.

open.q: Describe the two rib-cage movements ('pump-handle' and 'bucket-handle') produced by external intercostal contraction during inspiration.
accept: Pump-handle movement elevates the sternum/upper ribs to increase anteroposterior diameter; bucket-handle movement swings lower ribs outward to increase transverse diameter
Pump-handle increases AP diameter; bucket-handle increases transverse diameter

questions.q: Why is quiet expiration normally a completely passive process, and which muscles are recruited during forced expiration (such as coughing or maximal exercise)?
options: Quiet expiration uses elastic recoil; forced expiration recruits abdominal muscles and internal intercostals
Quiet expiration requires active abdominal contraction; forced expiration is passive
Quiet expiration is driven by the scalenes; forced expiration uses the diaphragm alone
Both quiet and forced expiration depend on external intercostal contraction
questions.explain: When inspiratory muscles relax at end-inspiration, stored elastic energy in lung elastin/collagen and alveolar surface tension recoils the lungs; forced expiration actively raises intra-abdominal pressure (pushing the diaphragm upward) and depresses the ribs. Quiet expiration follows relaxation of inspiratory muscles, allowing stored elastic energy in lung elastin/collagen and alveolar surface tension to recoil the lungs. Forced expiration recruits rectus abdominis, the obliques, transversus abdominis and internal intercostals; abdominal contraction raises intra-abdominal pressure and pushes the diaphragm upward.

open.q: Name the two major muscle groups recruited during active forced expiration.
accept: Abdominal muscles (rectus abdominis, obliques, transversus abdominis) and internal intercostal muscles
Abdominal wall muscles and internal intercostals

questions.q: Which accessory muscles are recruited during labored or forced inspiration (such as in acute severe asthma or COPD exacerbation)?
options: Internal intercostals and rectus abdominis
Sternocleidomastoid (elevates sternum), scalenes (elevate first two ribs), and pectoralis minor/serratus anterior
Transversus abdominis and pelvic floor muscles
Diaphragm and internal obliques only
questions.explain: Accessory inspiratory muscles lift the upper thoracic cage and sternum when airway resistance is high or minute ventilation increases markedly.

open.q: Name two accessory muscles of inspiration recruited during respiratory distress.
accept: Sternocleidomastoid and scalene muscles
Sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, pectoralis minor

questions.q: What is the normal intrapleural (intrathoracic) pressure at functional residual capacity (end of quiet expiration) and at the end of a normal quiet inspiration (relative to atmospheric pressure = 0 cmH2O)?
options: +5 cmH2O at rest, rising to +10 cmH2O during inspiration
-5 cmH2O at rest (FRC), becoming more negative to about -7.5 to -8 cmH2O during quiet inspiration
0 cmH2O at rest, rising to +3 cmH2O during inspiration
-20 cmH2O at rest, rising to 0 cmH2O during inspiration
questions.explain: At FRC, the inward elastic recoil of the lungs balances the outward spring of the thoracic wall, generating a subatmospheric intrapleural pressure of ~-5 cmH2O that deepens to ~-8 cmH2O as the chest wall expands during inspiration.

open.q: State the normal intrapleural pressure (in cmH2O relative to atmospheric pressure) at functional residual capacity and at end-quiet inspiration.
accept: -5 cmH2O at FRC and approximately -7.5 to -8 cmH2O at end-inspiration
-5 cmH2O at rest, -8 cmH2O during inspiration

questions.q: How do alveolar pressure (PA) and airflow behave at the exact midpoints of inspiration and expiration versus the end-inspiratory and end-expiratory pauses?
options: Mid-inspiration: PA ≈ −1; mid-expiration: +1; pauses: 0 cmH2O
Mid-inspiration: PA ≈ +1; mid-expiration: −1; pauses: 0 cmH2O
PA remains −5 cmH2O throughout inspiration and expiration
Airflow is maximal at pauses when PA equals atmospheric pressure
questions.explain: By Boyle's law (P1V1 = P2V2), thoracic expansion drops PA to ~-1 cmH2O to draw air in; once flow ceases at end-inspiration and end-expiration, PA equilibrates with atmospheric pressure (0 cmH2O). During inspiration, thoracic expansion lowers alveolar pressure to about −1 cmH2O and draws air inward. During expiration, PA rises to about +1 cmH2O and drives air outward. At end-inspiration and end-expiration, PA returns to atmospheric pressure (0) and airflow stops.

open.q: State the alveolar pressure (relative to atmospheric pressure) during mid-inspiration, end-inspiration, and mid-expiration.
accept: Mid-inspiration: -1 cmH2O; End-inspiration: 0 cmH2O; Mid-expiration: +1 cmH2O
-1 cmH2O, 0 cmH2O, +1 cmH2O

questions.q: How is 'transpulmonary pressure' (PTP) defined, and what physiological role does it serve?
options: PTP = PA − Ppl; the distending pressure that keeps alveoli open
PTP = Ppl − PA; the pressure that collapses alveoli
PTP = arterial PO2 − venous PO2; the pressure driving diffusion
PTP = tidal volume ÷ respiratory rate; the pressure driving ventilation
questions.explain: At FRC, PA = 0 cmH2O and Ppl = -5 cmH2O, so PTP = 0 - (-5) = +5 cmH2O; during quiet inspiration, PTP rises to +8 cmH2O to expand the alveoli. Transpulmonary pressure is alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure. At FRC, PA is about 0 and Ppl about −5 cmH2O, giving a PTP of +5 cmH2O; this distending pressure opposes elastic recoil.

open.q: Write the formula for transpulmonary pressure and calculate its value at functional residual capacity when alveolar pressure is 0 cmH2O and intrapleural pressure is -5 cmH2O.
accept: PTP = PA - Ppl (Alveolar pressure minus intrapleural pressure); +5 cmH2O
PA - Ppl = +5 cmH2O

questions.q: In a standing upright human at functional residual capacity, why is intrapleural pressure more negative at the lung apex (~-8 to -10 cmH2O) than at the lung base (~-2.5 cmH2O), and how does this affect regional ventilation?
options: Apical alveoli are more distended and less compliant; basal alveoli expand more during inspiration
Apical alveoli are smaller and more compliant, so they receive greater ventilation
Basal alveoli are more distended and less compliant, so they receive less ventilation
Gravity does not alter pleural pressure or regional ventilation
questions.explain: Because basal alveoli sit on the steeper part of the pressure-volume compliance curve at FRC, they expand more for a given pressure drop during inspiration, so regional ventilation is highest at the lung base and lowest at the apex. Gravity makes intrapleural pressure more negative at the apex (about −8 to −10 cmH2O) than at the base (about −2.5 cmH2O). Apical alveoli are already more expanded at FRC and lie on a flatter part of the compliance curve; basal alveoli are less expanded and more compliant, so they receive greater ventilation per unit volume.

open.q: Why do alveoli at the base of an upright lung receive greater ventilation per unit volume during quiet inspiration than alveoli at the lung apex?
accept: Gravity makes intrapleural pressure less negative at the base, leaving basal alveoli smaller at rest and on a steeper, more compliant portion of the pressure-volume curve so they expand more during inspiration
Basal alveoli are less distended at FRC and sit on a steeper, more compliant region of the compliance curve

questions.q: How is pulmonary compliance (CL) defined mathematically, and what is the normal compliance of the isolated human lungs versus the combined lung-chest wall respiratory system?
options: Compliance = ΔV/ΔP; lungs ≈0.2 L/cmH2O, combined system ≈0.1 L/cmH2O
Compliance = ΔP/ΔV; lungs ≈0.1 L/cmH2O, combined system ≈0.2 L/cmH2O
Compliance = airway resistance × respiratory rate; both systems ≈0.5 L/cmH2O
Combined lung-chest wall compliance is twice isolated lung compliance
questions.explain: Because the lungs and chest wall act in series, their elastances add (1/C_total = 1/C_lung + 1/C_chest wall), so combined compliance (~0.1 L/cmH2O) is half of isolated lung compliance (~0.2 L/cmH2O). Pulmonary compliance is the change in lung volume divided by the change in transpulmonary pressure (ΔV/ΔP). Isolated lung compliance is about 0.2 L/cmH2O (200 mL/cmH2O), while combined lung-chest wall compliance is about 0.1 L/cmH2O (100 mL/cmH2O), because the two elastances act in series.

open.q: Define lung compliance (CL) and state the approximate normal values for isolated lungs and for the combined lung-chest wall system.
accept: CL = Delta V / Delta P; ~0.2 L/cmH2O (200 mL/cmH2O) for lungs alone and ~0.1 L/cmH2O (100 mL/cmH2O) for the combined lung-chest wall system
Change in volume per unit change in pressure; 0.2 L/cmH2O (lungs) and 0.1 L/cmH2O (combined)

questions.q: How do emphysema and pulmonary fibrosis shift the static pressure-volume (compliance) curve of the lung?
options: Emphysema: ↑ compliance, ↓ recoil, ↑ FRC; fibrosis: ↓ compliance, ↑ recoil, ↓ FRC
Emphysema: ↓ compliance, ↑ recoil, ↓ FRC; fibrosis: ↑ compliance, ↓ recoil, ↑ FRC
Both diseases increase compliance and elastic recoil
Both diseases reduce compliance and elastic recoil equally
questions.explain: Emphysema destroys alveolar elastin fibers (high compliance, poor outward expiratory recoil, air trapping), whereas fibrosis deposits stiff interstitial collagen (low compliance, high work of breathing). Emphysema destroys alveolar elastin, increasing compliance while reducing elastic recoil and promoting air trapping and a higher FRC. Fibrosis deposits stiff interstitial collagen, reducing compliance, increasing elastic recoil and lowering FRC.

open.q: Compare how emphysema and pulmonary fibrosis alter lung compliance, elastic recoil, and functional residual capacity (FRC).
accept: Emphysema increases compliance, decreases elastic recoil, and increases FRC; pulmonary fibrosis decreases compliance, increases elastic recoil, and decreases FRC
Emphysema: high compliance/low recoil/high FRC; Fibrosis: low compliance/high recoil/low FRC

questions.q: What is 'hysteresis' on a static lung pressure-volume loop, and why is it dramatically reduced when an excised lung is inflated with isotonic saline instead of air?
options: Hysteresis is the difference between inflation and deflation pressure-volume curves; saline reduces it by removing the air-liquid surface tension
Hysteresis is airway closure during inspiration and is increased by saline
Hysteresis occurs only in skeletal muscle and is unrelated to lung mechanics
Saline increases alveolar surface tension and makes the lung markedly stiffer
questions.explain: During air inflation, higher pressure is needed to overcome surface tension and recruit closed alveoli, whereas during deflation surfactant concentrates and lowers surface tension; saline eliminates surface tension, leaving only tissue elastin/collagen recoil.

open.q: Why does inflating an excised lung with saline rather than air reduce the pressure needed for inflation and nearly abolish pressure-volume hysteresis?
accept: Saline eliminates the alveolar air-liquid interface and surface tension, which normally accounts for roughly two-thirds of lung elastic recoil and hysteresis
Elimination of air-liquid surface tension leaves only tissue elasticity

questions.sub: Alveolar Surface Tension, Laplace's Law, and Surfactant
questions.q: According to the Law of Laplace for a spherical alveolus (P = 2T / r), what would happen to small alveoli communicating with large alveoli if surface tension (T) were constant?
options: Large alveoli would empty into small alveoli
Small alveoli (smaller radius r) would generate higher inward collapsing pressure (P) and empty/collapse into larger alveoli (atelectasis)
Both small and large alveoli would have identical collapsing pressure regardless of radius
Surface tension would force alveoli to expand infinitely
questions.explain: Because P = 2T/r, if T remained constant, halving radius r would double collapsing pressure P, causing small alveoli to empty into large ones.

open.q: Write the Law of Laplace for a spherical alveolus and explain why constant surface tension would destabilize alveoli of different sizes.
accept: P = 2T / r; with constant surface tension (T), smaller alveoli (smaller r) have higher collapsing pressure (P) and would empty into larger alveoli
P = 2T/r; smaller radius produces greater inward collapsing pressure

questions.sub: Alveolar Surface Tension, Laplace's Law, and Surfactant
questions.q: Which alveolar cells synthesize pulmonary surfactant, what is its major phospholipid component, and how does surfactant stabilize alveoli of varying radii?
options: Type I pneumocytes; sphingomyelin; raises surface tension during expiration
Type II pneumocytes produce DPPC-rich surfactant, which lowers surface tension and stabilises small alveoli
Alveolar macrophages; cholesterol; relaxes bronchial smooth muscle
Goblet cells; mucin; prevents water evaporation from the pleural cavity
questions.explain: Amphipathic DPPC inserts between water molecules at the air-liquid interface, disrupting hydrogen bonds; as an alveolus shrinks, DPPC surface concentration rises, dropping T dramatically to prevent end-expiratory collapse and reduce work of breathing.

open.q: Name the cell type that produces pulmonary surfactant, its primary phospholipid constituent, and three physiological functions of surfactant.
accept: Type II alveolar epithelial cells (pneumocytes); dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC); increases lung compliance (reduces work of breathing), stabilizes alveoli of different sizes (prevents atelectasis), and keeps alveoli dry (opposes transudation of fluid)
Type II pneumocytes; DPPC; increases compliance, prevents atelectasis, and prevents pulmonary edema

questions.sub: Alveolar Surface Tension, Laplace's Law, and Surfactant
questions.q: How does pulmonary surfactant prevent pulmonary edema (keep alveoli dry)?
options: Surfactant lowers surface tension, reducing inward suction that draws fluid into alveoli
Surfactant raises surface tension, preventing fluid entry by increasing alveolar pressure
Surfactant closes pulmonary capillary junctions to stop filtration
Surfactant increases pulmonary venous pressure to oppose oedema
questions.explain: High unopposed surface tension creates negative interstitial/alveolar hydrostatic pressure pulling plasma transudate across the alveolar-capillary barrier (forming hyaline membranes in neonatal RDS). High unopposed alveolar surface tension creates an inward suction force and lowers interstitial/alveolar hydrostatic pressure, favouring fluid movement from pulmonary capillaries into alveoli. Surfactant reduces this surface tension.

open.q: Explain how surfactant deficiency promotes fluid transudation into alveoli.
accept: High unopposed alveolar surface tension creates an inward suction force that lowers interstitial/alveolar hydrostatic pressure and draws fluid out of pulmonary capillaries
Elevated surface tension pulls fluid from capillaries across the alveolar-capillary membrane

questions.q: According to Poiseuille's law for laminar airflow (R = 8 * viscosity * length / pi * r^4), if bronchoconstriction reduces airway radius (r) by half (50%), by what factor does airway resistance increase?
options: 2-fold
4-fold
8-fold
16-fold
questions.explain: Because resistance is inversely proportional to the fourth power of radius (1 / r^4), halving radius increases resistance by 2^4 = 16-fold.

open.q: State the proportional relationship between airway resistance (R) and airway radius (r) in Poiseuille's law, and calculate the resistance change if radius decreases by 50%.
accept: R is proportional to 1 / r^4; halving radius increases airway resistance 16-fold
Inverse fourth power of radius; 16-fold increase

questions.q: Which anatomical region of the tracheobronchial tree contributes the GREATEST fraction of total airway resistance in a healthy human lung, and why?
options: Terminal bronchioles, because their small individual diameter dominates total resistance
Medium-sized segmental and lobar bronchi (generations 3–7)
Alveolar ducts, because their walls contain smooth muscle
The trachea alone, because it has the narrowest lumen
questions.explain: Because resistances in parallel add reciprocally (1/R_total = 1/R1 + 1/R2 + ...), the millions of small peripheral airways (<2 mm, the 'silent zone') contribute <10-20% of total resistance, while medium bronchi (~generations 4-7) represent the bottleneck. Although individual peripheral bronchioles are narrow, they are arranged in millions of parallel pathways with a very large total cross-sectional area. Their combined resistance is therefore low; medium-sized bronchi are the main contributors to total airway resistance in healthy lungs.

open.q: Why do small peripheral airways (<2 mm diameter) contribute relatively little to total airway resistance in healthy lungs despite their narrow individual diameters?
accept: They branch extensively in parallel, creating a massive total cross-sectional area that lowers combined parallel resistance
Parallel arrangement of millions of small airways yields a very large total cross-sectional area

questions.q: How do lung volume, autonomic neurotransmitters, and local alveolar PCO2 regulate bronchial smooth muscle tone and airway resistance?
options: High lung volume, β2 stimulation and high PCO2 dilate airways; M3, histamine, leukotrienes and low PCO2 constrict them
Vagal M3 stimulation dilates airways; β2 stimulation and high PCO2 constrict them
Low lung volume and low PCO2 dilate airways; histamine reduces resistance
All autonomic and local signals produce bronchodilation
questions.explain: At high lung volumes, surrounding elastic parenchyma pulls radially on airway walls (radial traction), widening airways; local hypocapnia constricts airways to divert ventilation away from underperfused alveoli. High lung volume increases radial traction on airway walls. β2-adrenergic stimulation and high local alveolar PCO2 promote bronchodilation; parasympathetic M3 stimulation, histamine, leukotrienes and local hypocapnia promote bronchoconstriction.

open.q: State the effects on airway smooth muscle tone of: (1) high lung volume, (2) sympathetic beta-2 stimulation, (3) parasympathetic M3 stimulation, and (4) local alveolar hypocapnia (low PCO2).
accept: 1) Bronchodilation (radial traction), 2) Bronchodilation, 3) Bronchoconstriction, 4) Bronchoconstriction
High volume and beta-2 dilate; M3 and low PCO2 constrict

questions.sub: Dynamic Airway Compression and Equal Pressure Point
questions.q: What is 'dynamic airway compression' during a forced expiration, and what is the 'equal pressure point' (EPP)?
options: Beyond the EPP, intrapleural pressure exceeds airway pressure and compresses non-cartilaginous airways
Beyond the EPP, airway pressure exceeds intrapleural pressure and dilates all airways
Dynamic compression occurs only during quiet inspiration
The EPP is the point where alveolar and arterial oxygen tensions become equal
questions.explain: As air flows from alveoli toward the mouth during forced expiration, resistive pressure drops along the airway; once intraluminal pressure falls below surrounding positive intrapleural pressure, non-cartilaginous airways compress, limiting maximal flow regardless of greater expiratory effort. During forced expiration, intraluminal pressure falls along the airway as gas flows toward the mouth. At the equal-pressure point it equals intrapleural pressure; downstream, surrounding pleural pressure can compress collapsible, non-cartilaginous airways and limit flow.

open.q: Define the 'equal pressure point' during forced expiration and explain why expiratory flow becomes effort-independent over the lower two-thirds of vital capacity.
accept: Point along the airway where intraluminal pressure equals surrounding intrapleural pressure; downstream of this point, positive intrapleural pressure compresses non-cartilaginous airways so further muscular effort increases both driving pressure and airway compression equally
Location where airway pressure equals intrapleural pressure; downstream dynamic compression caps maximal expiratory flow

questions.sub: Dynamic Airway Compression and Equal Pressure Point
questions.q: Why do patients with severe emphysema instinctively breathe out through 'pursed lips'?
options: Pursed-lip breathing raises airway pressure and delays small-airway collapse
It lowers alveolar pressure and accelerates small-airway emptying
It relaxes the diaphragm and reduces inspiratory effort
It increases anatomical dead space to reduce CO2 loss
questions.explain: In emphysema, loss of elastic recoil lowers alveolar driving pressure and causes early dynamic collapse of small airways; creating back-pressure at the lips keeps intraluminal pressure higher than intrapleural pressure longer, stenting airways open. In emphysema, loss of elastic recoil lowers alveolar driving pressure and promotes early dynamic collapse of small airways. Resistance at the lips creates expiratory back-pressure, maintaining intraluminal pressure and shifting the equal-pressure point toward larger, cartilage-supported airways.

open.q: Explain the mechanical benefit of pursed-lip breathing in patients with emphysema.
accept: Creates positive back-pressure inside the airways that shifts the equal pressure point toward larger, cartilage-supported bronchi and prevents premature dynamic collapse of small airways
Raises intraluminal airway pressure to prevent dynamic airway collapse during expiration

questions.sub: Work of Breathing and Closing Capacity
questions.q: What are the two major components of the mechanical work of breathing during quiet respiration, and what percentage of total resting body oxygen consumption does quiet breathing normally require?
options: Elastic and resistive work; quiet breathing uses about 1–3% of resting VO2
Elastic and resistive work; quiet breathing uses about 25–30% of resting VO2
Only resistive work; quiet breathing uses about 10% of resting VO2
Only elastic work; quiet breathing uses no oxygen
questions.explain: Normally breathing is remarkably energy-efficient (~1-3% of resting O2 uptake), but in severe COPD or restrictive fibrosis, work of breathing can rise to >25-30% of total O2 consumption, precipitating ventilatory muscle fatigue. Elastic work overcomes lung/chest-wall recoil and surface tension; resistive work overcomes airway resistance and tissue viscosity. Quiet breathing normally consumes only about 1–3% of resting oxygen uptake, but this can rise markedly in severe obstructive or restrictive disease.

open.q: Name the two main components of mechanical work during inspiration and state the approximate percentage of resting body oxygen uptake consumed by quiet breathing.
accept: Elastic work (compliance work) and flow-resistive work; approximately 1 to 3% (less than 5%) of resting oxygen consumption
Elastic recoil work and airway resistance work; ~1-3% of resting VO2

questions.sub: Work of Breathing and Closing Capacity
questions.q: How do patients with restrictive lung disease (low compliance, high elastic work) versus obstructive lung disease (high airway resistance, high resistive work) alter their breathing pattern to minimize work of breathing?
options: Restrictive disease: rapid, shallow breathing; obstructive disease: slow, deep breathing
Restrictive disease: slow, deep breathing; obstructive disease: rapid, shallow breathing
Both diseases produce rapid, deep breathing to minimise work
Both diseases produce slow, shallow breathing regardless of mechanics
questions.explain: Because elastic work scales with the square of tidal volume (V_T^2 / 2C) while resistive work scales with airflow velocity (frequency), each group unconsciously selects the rate-depth combination minimizing total energy cost. Restrictive patients reduce tidal volume and increase respiratory rate to limit elastic work. Obstructive patients slow their respiratory rate and use larger tidal volumes to reduce flow-resistive work and allow more time for expiration.

open.q: Contrast the spontaneous breathing patterns (respiratory rate and tidal volume) adopted to minimize work of breathing in restrictive versus obstructive lung disease.
accept: Restrictive disease: rapid, shallow breaths (high rate, low tidal volume) to reduce elastic work; Obstructive disease: slow, deep breaths (low rate, higher tidal volume) to reduce flow-resistive work
Rapid shallow breathing in restrictive disease vs slow deep breathing in obstructive disease

questions.sub: Work of Breathing and Closing Capacity
questions.q: What is 'closing capacity' (CC), and what happens when closing capacity exceeds functional residual capacity (FRC), such as with advancing age or supine posture?
options: Closing capacity is the volume at which small airways begin to close; if it exceeds FRC, airway closure occurs during tidal breathing
Closing capacity is the maximum volume inhaled after a forced expiration
Closing capacity is always zero in older adults
When closing capacity exceeds FRC, arterial oxygen tension rises
questions.explain: As elastic recoil declines with age, closing capacity rises from ~30% of TLC in young adults to exceed FRC (~45% of TLC) around age 65 upright (and ~44 supine), explaining the age-related decline in resting PaO2.

open.q: Define closing capacity and explain why arterial PO2 declines when closing capacity exceeds functional residual capacity (FRC).
accept: Lung volume at which dependent small airways begin to close during expiration; when CC > FRC, basal airways close during tidal breathing, creating low V/Q regions (shunt-like effect) and lowering PaO2
Volume where dependent airways collapse; closure during tidal breathing impairs basal ventilation and causes V/Q mismatch

questions.sub: Lung Volumes, Capacities, and Dead Space
questions.q: Which of the four standard static lung volumes CANNOT be measured directly by simple spirometry, and how is it measured clinically?
options: Tidal volume; measured by pulse oximetry
Inspiratory reserve volume; measured by capnography
Residual volume (and FRC/TLC) requires indirect measurement, e.g. plethysmography or gas dilution
Expiratory reserve volume; measured by arterial blood gas
questions.explain: Because residual volume (~1.2 L) remains in the lungs even after maximal forced expiration, spirometry only measures exhaled/inhaled volume changes; body plethysmography (using Boyle's law) measures all thoracic gas including trapped bullous gas. Residual volume remains in the lungs after maximal expiration and cannot be measured by simple spirometry. Functional residual capacity and total lung capacity also contain RV and require indirect methods such as helium dilution, nitrogen washout or body plethysmography.

open.q: Name the lung volume and two lung capacities that cannot be measured by simple spirometry, and list two indirect methods used to measure them.
accept: Residual volume (RV), functional residual capacity (FRC), and total lung capacity (TLC); measured by helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography
RV, FRC, and TLC; helium dilution, nitrogen washout, or body plethysmography

questions.sub: Lung Volumes, Capacities, and Dead Space
questions.q: How do 'anatomical dead space' and 'physiological dead space' differ in a healthy person versus a patient with pulmonary embolism?
options: Anatomical dead space is conducting airways; physiological dead space also includes ventilated but underperfused alveoli
Anatomical dead space is perfused alveoli; physiological dead space excludes alveolar dead space
Both terms describe the same volume in health and pulmonary embolism
Pulmonary embolism increases anatomical dead space by collapsing the trachea
questions.explain: Physiological dead space (VD) is calculated via the Bohr equation: VD / VT = (PaCO2 - PECO2) / PaCO2; pulmonary embolism blocks capillary perfusion to ventilated alveoli, creating large alveolar dead space. Physiological dead space equals anatomical dead space plus alveolar dead space. Pulmonary embolism blocks perfusion to ventilated alveoli, increasing alveolar dead space; the Bohr equation estimates the physiological dead-space fraction.

open.q: Define anatomical dead space and physiological dead space, and state the equation (Bohr's equation) used to calculate physiological dead space.
accept: Anatomical dead space is the volume of conducting airways (~150 mL); physiological dead space is anatomical plus alveolar dead space; Bohr equation: VD/VT = (PaCO2 - PECO2) / PaCO2
Conducting airway volume vs total non-gas-exchanging ventilated volume; VD = VT * (PaCO2 - PECO2) / PaCO2

questions.sub: Lung Volumes, Capacities, and Dead Space
questions.q: Given a tidal volume (VT) of 500 mL, anatomical dead space (VD) of 150 mL, and respiratory rate of 12 breaths/min, what is the minute ventilation (VE) versus alveolar ventilation (VA)?
options: Minute ventilation = 6,000 mL/min (6.0 L/min); Alveolar ventilation = 4,200 mL/min (4.2 L/min)
Minute ventilation = 4,200 mL/min; Alveolar ventilation = 6,000 mL/min
Both minute ventilation and alveolar ventilation equal 1,800 mL/min
Alveolar ventilation = 7,800 mL/min
questions.explain: VE = VT * f = 500 * 12 = 6,000 mL/min, whereas VA = (VT - VD) * f = (500 - 150) * 12 = 350 * 12 = 4,200 mL/min; rapid shallow breathing (e.g., VT 200 mL, f 30) keeps VE at 6,000 mL/min but drops VA to (200 - 150) * 30 = 1,500 mL/min!

open.q: Calculate alveolar ventilation (VA) for a patient with tidal volume 300 mL, dead space 150 mL, and respiratory rate 20 breaths/min.
accept: 3,000 mL/min (3.0 L/min)
3000 mL/min

questions.q: A premature male neonate born at 28 weeks of gestation develops tachypnea, nasal flaring, intercostal retractions, expiratory grunting, and cyanosis within 2 hours of birth. Chest radiograph reveals diffuse ground-glass reticulogranular infiltrates with air bronchograms. What is the underlying pathophysiology of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS)?
options: Surfactant deficiency raises surface tension, lowers compliance and causes alveolar atelectasis
Excess surfactant lowers surface tension and causes alveolar overdistension
Phrenic nerve paralysis causes isolated loss of expiratory effort
Alpha-globin deficiency causes diffuse alveolar collapse
questions.explain: Mature surfactant production surges after ~34-35 weeks gestation (accelerated by maternal antenatal betamethasone); surfactant deficiency collapses alveoli (Laplace's law), treated with CPAP and exogenous intratracheal surfactant. Immature type II pneumocytes produce inadequate pulmonary surfactant, often with a low lecithin-to-sphingomyelin ratio. Increased surface tension lowers compliance, causes diffuse microatelectasis and intrapulmonary right-to-left shunting. Antenatal corticosteroids accelerate surfactant maturation; treatment may include CPAP and exogenous surfactant.

open.q: Explain the pathophysiology of neonatal respiratory distress syndrome (NRDS) and why expiratory grunting helps these infants.
accept: Surfactant deficiency in immature Type II pneumocytes elevates alveolar surface tension, reducing compliance and causing widespread atelectasis; grunting against a partially closed glottis generates positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) to keep alveoli open
Lack of surfactant increases collapsing surface tension; glottic grunting creates PEEP to prevent alveolar collapse

questions.q: A 23-year-old tall, thin man presents with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and dyspnea. Examination reveals absent breath sounds, hyperresonance to percussion on the right, and tracheal deviation to the left. What happens to ipsilateral intrapleural pressure, lung volume, and chest wall volume in a pneumothorax?
options: Pleural air removes negative pressure: the lung collapses inward and the chest wall recoils outward
Pleural air makes pressure more negative, expanding the lung and drawing the chest wall inward
The affected lung expands while the opposite chest wall collapses
Transpulmonary pressure rises and both lungs inflate
questions.explain: Normally, the lung pulls inward and the chest wall springs outward across the sealed negative-pressure pleural space; breaking the pleural seal lets each structure recoil to its own equilibrium volume (collapsed lung, expanded hemithorax). Normally, the lung recoils inward while the chest wall springs outward across the sealed negative-pressure pleural space. When air enters the pleural cavity, intrapleural pressure rises toward atmospheric pressure (or becomes positive in tension pneumothorax), allowing the lung to collapse and the ipsilateral chest wall to expand.

open.q: Describe what happens to the volume of the affected lung and the volume of the ipsilateral chest wall when air enters the pleural space in a pneumothorax.
accept: The affected lung collapses inward (decreases in volume) and the ipsilateral chest wall springs outward (increases in volume) as negative intrapleural pressure is lost
Lung collapses inward; chest wall expands outward

questions.q: A 58-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history presents with progressive exertional dyspnea, barrel chest, hyperresonant lung fields, prolonged expiratory phase, and spirometry showing FEV1/FVC of 52% (normal >70-75%) and elevated TLC and RV. What is the mechanical basis of his barrel chest and reduced FEV1/FVC?
options: Loss of elastic recoil increases compliance and causes hyperinflation; reduced radial traction promotes expiratory airway collapse
Excess collagen stiffens the lungs, increasing TLC and causing a barrel chest
Surfactant overproduction obstructs the trachea and lowers residual volume
Phrenic nerve paralysis increases elastic recoil and raises FEV1/FVC
questions.explain: In emphysema, weak inward lung elastic recoil shifts FRC upward (chest wall springs outward into a barrel configuration) and diminishes radial tethering of small airways, markedly slowing forced expiration (low FEV1 and low FEV1/FVC).

open.q: Explain why functional residual capacity (FRC) and total lung capacity (TLC) increase in emphysema.
accept: Destruction of lung elastin reduces inward elastic recoil of the lungs, shifting the balance point against outward chest wall recoil to a larger resting lung volume (hyperinflation)
Decreased inward lung elastic recoil allows the outward spring of the chest wall to expand resting lung volume

questions.q: A 64-year-old retired sandblaster presents with progressive dry cough, dyspnea, bibasilar fine end-inspiratory crackles, and spirometry showing FVC 54% predicted, FEV1 58% predicted, FEV1/FVC ratio of 86%, and TLC 56% predicted. Why is the FEV1/FVC ratio normal or elevated in restrictive pulmonary fibrosis?
options: Fibrosis lowers compliance but increases elastic recoil, helping preserve airway patency and FEV1/FVC
Fibrosis increases compliance and reduces elastic recoil, lowering FEV1/FVC
Fibrosis selectively reduces FEV1 while preserving FVC
Fibrosis causes severe bronchoconstriction with increased residual volume
questions.explain: In restrictive parenchymal fibrosis, both FVC and FEV1 fall proportionally (keeping FEV1/FVC normal or >80%) because high elastic recoil and radial tethering maintain high expiratory flow relative to the reduced lung volume. In restrictive parenchymal fibrosis, both FEV1 and FVC fall, often proportionally, so the ratio remains normal or rises. Increased elastic recoil and radial tethering help maintain airway calibre and expiratory flow despite reduced lung volumes.

open.q: Explain why the FEV1/FVC ratio is typically normal or increased (>80%) in restrictive lung diseases such as idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis.
accept: Both FEV1 and FVC are reduced proportionally due to stiff, low-compliance lungs, while increased elastic recoil provides strong radial traction that keeps airways open during forced expiration
Proportional reduction in FEV1 and FVC plus high elastic recoil maintaining airway patency

questions.q: A 34-year-old woman sustains a complete traumatic spinal cord transection at the C2 vertebral level in a motor vehicle collision and immediately develops apneic respiratory arrest requiring mechanical ventilation. Why does a C2 transection cause complete paralysis of breathing whereas a C6 transection spares quiet diaphragmatic breathing?
options: A C2 lesion interrupts descending drive to phrenic motor neurons (C3–C5); a C6 lesion usually spares diaphragmatic innervation
The phrenic nerve arises from T1–T6, so both lesions spare diaphragmatic breathing
A C2 lesion affects only the vagus nerve and leaves respiratory muscles intact
Intercostal muscles alone maintain normal quiet breathing after a C2 lesion
questions.explain: High cervical lesions above C3 sever descending respiratory drive from the medullary ventral/dorsal respiratory groups to phrenic motor neurons (C3-C5), whereas lesions below C5 paralyze intercostal and abdominal muscles while preserving phrenic diaphragmatic inspiration.

open.q: Contrast the respiratory consequences of a complete spinal cord injury at C2 versus C6.
accept: C2 lesion interrupts descending drive above C3-C5, paralyzing the diaphragm and all respiratory muscles (apnea); C6 lesion spares phrenic nerve (C3-C5) innervation of the diaphragm while paralyzing intercostal and abdominal muscles
C2 causes diaphragmatic paralysis and respiratory arrest; C6 preserves diaphragmatic breathing via intact C3-C5 phrenic roots

questions.q: A patient with pulmonary fibrosis has stiff lungs and increased work of breathing. Which change in lung mechanics is expected?
options: Reduced lung compliance
Increased lung compliance
Reduced elastic recoil
Reduced surface tension due to excess surfactant
questions.explain: Pulmonary fibrosis increases elastic stiffness and reduces lung compliance, so a greater transpulmonary pressure is needed to produce a given change in lung volume.

open.q: What happens to lung compliance in pulmonary fibrosis?
accept: It is reduced
Decreased lung compliance

questions.q: A premature neonate develops respiratory distress due to surfactant deficiency. Which effect of surfactant is lost?
options: Reduction of alveolar surface tension, especially in small alveoli
Increase in alveolar surface tension during expiration
Increase in pulmonary capillary hydrostatic pressure
Prevention of oxygen diffusion across the alveolar membrane
questions.explain: Pulmonary surfactant reduces surface tension and helps stabilise alveoli, particularly smaller alveoli, reducing the tendency to collapse and decreasing work of breathing.

open.q: What is the main physical effect of pulmonary surfactant?
accept: It reduces alveolar surface tension
